Q171617.t: Coffee money, twin motorways and an opera composer
Q171617.s: Two motorways run side by side out of São Paulo and end in a big, sprawling grid on the rolling plateau: that is Campinas. In the 19th century it was one of the richest coffee towns in Brazil. Today universities, research labs and a busy cargo airport have taken coffee's place, and cane fields fill the country around.
Q171617.w: A large pale sprawl on hilly farmland north-west of São Paulo, threaded by two parallel motorways; Viracopos airport's runway to the south-west.
f: Composer Carlos Gomes was born here in 1836; his opera Il Guarany premiered at La Scala in Milan in 1870.
The Anhanguera and Bandeirantes motorways link Campinas with São Paulo, about 90 km away.
Viracopos airport, south-west of the centre, is one of Brazil's busiest air-cargo hubs.

q.q: Which composer of the opera Il Guarany was born in Campinas?

Q5092.t: The harbour that gave America its anthem
Q5092.s: Follow the Chesapeake Bay north until a river estuary splits into fingers of water: Baltimore wraps around their tips. In 1814 British ships bombarded Fort McHenry at the harbour mouth all night, and seeing the flag still flying at dawn, Francis Scott Key wrote the words of 'The Star-Spangled Banner'. Today the old harbour front is lined with museums and moored ships.
Q5092.w: A city clasping a branching estuary on the west side of the Chesapeake Bay, about 60 km north-east of Washington.
f: The Baltimore and Ohio, chartered in 1827, was one of the first railways in the United States.
Edgar Allan Poe died in Baltimore in 1849; the city's football team, the Ravens, is named after his poem.
Baseball's Babe Ruth was born in Baltimore in 1895.

q.q: Which song was inspired by the defence of Baltimore's Fort McHenry?

Q165972.t: Canals like a comb, the Everglades at its back
Q165972.s: Look closely at the shore: rows of narrow finger islands jut into the water like the teeth of a comb, each lined with houses and boat docks. These canals earned Fort Lauderdale its nickname, the 'Venice of America'. A thin barrier beach faces the Atlantic, and inland the suburbs stop abruptly at the flat, grassy Everglades.
Q165972.w: Comb-like canals along the coast north of Miami; the deep-water cruise port by the ocean inlet; flat green Everglades to the west.
f: The city grew around a fort built in 1838 and named after Major William Lauderdale.
Port Everglades, at the city's south edge, is one of the busiest cruise ports in the world.
Westward, the suburbs end at long levees that fence off the Everglades wetlands.

q.q: What nickname do Fort Lauderdale's many canals earn it?

Q16739.t: Oil wells disguised as tropical islands
Q16739.s: A long stone breakwater fences off the bay, and behind it container terminals spread over land reclaimed from the sea. Look offshore for four small islands: palm trees and colourful towers there hide working oil wells. Long Beach and its twin port of Los Angeles handle a large share of America's trade with Asia.
Q16739.w: Straight breakwaters enclosing San Pedro Bay at the southern end of the Los Angeles sprawl; grids of container docks behind them.
f: The ocean liner Queen Mary has been moored here as a hotel since 1967.
The four oil islands off the beach were built in the 1960s and dressed up to look like resort islands.
Together the ports of Long Beach and Los Angeles form the busiest container port complex in the US.

q.q: Which famous ocean liner is permanently moored in Long Beach?

Q62823.t: Where Colombia's great river finally meets the sea
Q62823.s: The Magdalena has flowed some 1,500 km from the Andes by the time it reaches Barranquilla, and here its brown water spills into the blue Caribbean. The city lines the west bank just before the mouth. Every year before Lent it throws one of the largest carnivals in the world, a feast of costumes, masks and cumbia.
Q62823.w: A wide brown river entering the Caribbean between long jetties; the city on its west bank; a large lagoon beyond the river to the east.
f: The Carnival of Barranquilla was proclaimed a UNESCO masterpiece of intangible heritage in 2003.
SCADTA, the airline that later became Avianca, was founded here in 1919.
The river mouth is called Bocas de Ceniza, 'Mouths of Ash', for its grey, silty water.

q.q: Which river meets the Caribbean at Barranquilla?

Q486168.t: A city pressed against a mountain wall and a fault
Q486168.s: The sprawl of Los Angeles runs east until it slams into a steep wall of mountains: that edge is San Bernardino. Along the foot of the slope runs the San Andreas Fault. North-west, a deep notch — the Cajon Pass — carries the railway and the freeway to the desert. And in 1940 two brothers opened a drive-in here called McDonald's.
Q486168.w: A grid of suburbs ending sharply at dark, steep mountains; a pass cutting north-west through them; in winter, snow on the peaks to the east.
f: Richard and Maurice McDonald opened their first restaurant in San Bernardino in 1940.
San Gorgonio Mountain, about 3,500 m, is the highest peak in Southern California.
Old Route 66 entered the Los Angeles basin through the Cajon Pass and San Bernardino.

q.q: Which fast-food chain began in San Bernardino in 1940?

Q81882.t: Latin America's busiest port, under a wall of forest
Q81882.s: A winding channel lined with docks, a long curve of beach, and behind it all a green escarpment rising almost straight up: that is Santos. São Paulo sits on the plateau above, and much of what Brazil sells to the world leaves through this port. Coffee made the city rich; football made it famous.
Q81882.w: A flat island city at the foot of the steep, forested Serra do Mar, south-east of São Paulo; docks along a winding channel.
f: Pelé played for Santos FC from 1956 to 1974.
Santos shares its island with São Vicente, founded in 1532 as the first Portuguese town in Brazil.
The old Coffee Exchange, where Brazil's crop was once priced, is now a coffee museum.

q.q: Which football legend played most of his career for Santos FC?

Q168376.t: An island capital guarding an iron-ore port
Q168376.s: Vitória is built on a hilly island in a bay, tied to the mainland by bridges, with granite hills poking up between the neighbourhoods. The state capital of Espírito Santo, it was founded by the Portuguese in the 16th century. On the island's northern edge, one of the world's biggest iron-ore terminals loads ships bound for Asia and Europe.
Q168376.w: A rocky island in a bay on the Atlantic coast, linked by bridges to the mainland; Vila Velha across the water to the south.
f: It is one of three Brazilian state capitals on an island, with Florianópolis and São Luís.
The clay pots of Goiabeiras, used for local moqueca, were the first craft listed as Brazil's intangible heritage, in 2002.
Iron ore reaches the Tubarão port by rail from the mines of Minas Gerais.

q.q: Vitória is the capital of which Brazilian state?

Q42763.t: Tobacco capital of the fertile Cibao valley
Q42763.s: In the green heart of the Dominican Republic, between two mountain ranges, lies the broad Cibao valley, and Santiago is its capital in all but name. Tobacco from these fields rolls into some of the world's most prized cigars. The city is the country's second largest; its full name honours the thirty caballeros said to have settled it.
Q42763.w: A large city in a wide green valley between the island's central mountains and a lower northern range; a river curving past its west side.
f: The Dominican Republic is one of the world's leading exporters of premium cigars, most of them made around Santiago.
Pico Duarte, 3,098 m and the highest peak in the Caribbean, rises in the Cordillera Central south-west of the city.
The Yaque del Norte river flows past the city on its way to the Atlantic.

q.q: Which valley is Santiago de los Caballeros the heart of?

Q209034.t: Mexico's highest state capital, under a broken volcano
Q209034.s: Toluca sits at about 2,660 m, higher than any other state capital in Mexico, on a broad valley west of Mexico City. South-west of the city stands the Nevado de Toluca, an old volcano whose crater has been torn open on one side. Inside it lie two lakes, and in winter the rim often turns white.
Q209034.w: A city on a flat, high valley; to the south-west a large volcano with a broken, often snowy crater rim.
f: The Nevado de Toluca rises to about 4,680 m, one of the highest peaks in Mexico.
The two crater lakes are called the Lake of the Sun and the Lake of the Moon.
The Lerma River, which flows on to Lake Chapala, rises from springs in the Toluca valley.

q.q: What are the two lakes inside the Nevado de Toluca crater called?

Q17042.t: The working shore of San Francisco Bay
Q17042.s: Across the bay from San Francisco, the giant cranes of the Port of Oakland line the waterfront, loading ships for the Pacific. Behind them the city climbs to wooded hills. In its middle is a round lake: Lake Merritt, a tidal lagoon that became America's first official wildlife refuge in 1870. The Bay Bridge ties Oakland to the city opposite.
Q17042.w: The east shore of San Francisco Bay: container cranes along the estuary, a small lake in the centre, the Bay Bridge heading west.
f: Lake Merritt was declared a wildlife refuge in 1870, the first such official refuge in the United States.
Writer Jack London spent much of his youth on the Oakland waterfront.
The Bay Bridge reaches San Francisco by way of Yerba Buena Island, in mid-bay.

q.q: Which Oakland lagoon became America's first official wildlife refuge?

Q178725.t: The city with the best view of Rio
Q178725.s: Guanabara Bay has two shores. Rio de Janeiro gets the fame; Niterói, on the eastern side, gets the view of Sugarloaf and Corcovado across the water. A bridge some 13 km long crosses the bay between them. Niterói traces its founding to 1573 and the Temiminó chief Araribóia, and its ocean beaches face the open Atlantic.
Q178725.w: The eastern shore of Guanabara Bay, opposite Rio; a long bridge crossing the bay; green granite hills behind the beaches.
f: The Rio–Niterói Bridge is about 13 km long, one of the longest in the Southern Hemisphere.
The name Niterói comes from Tupi and is usually translated as 'hidden water'.
Oscar Niemeyer's Contemporary Art Museum, shaped like a flying saucer, perches on a cliff above the bay.

q.q: Which bay separates Niterói from Rio de Janeiro?

Q49259.t: Watch the road dive under the bay
Q49259.s: At the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay, look for a thin line crossing open water that suddenly vanishes: the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel dives underground at two shipping channels. Virginia Beach lies at its southern end, a resort strip facing the Atlantic. Just here, at Cape Henry, the English colonists of 1607 first stepped ashore.
Q49259.w: Where the Chesapeake Bay meets the Atlantic: a long causeway crossing the bay mouth, a straight ocean beach running south.
f: The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel is about 28 km long from shore to shore.
The Jamestown colonists landed at Cape Henry in April 1607 before sailing up the James River.
Virginia Beach is the most populous city in Virginia.

q.q: Where did the Jamestown colonists first land in 1607?

Q189128.t: Mexico's shoe capital on the high Bajío plain
Q189128.s: If you own Mexican leather boots, there's a good chance they came from here. León is a big industrial city on the high Bajío plain, surrounded by a patchwork of farmland, and it has made shoes, belts and saddles for generations. Founded in 1576, it now honours two independence heroes, the Aldama brothers, in its name.
Q189128.w: A large city on a flat, farmed plain, with low mountains rising to its north; Guanajuato's hills to the south-east.
f: León is the centre of Mexico's footwear and leather industry.
The city was founded in 1576 as the Villa de León.
Juan and Ignacio Aldama fought alongside Miguel Hidalgo in the independence war that began in 1810.

q.q: What is León, Mexico, best known for making?

Q41819.t: One name, two states, two great rivers
Q41819.s: Where the Kansas River flows into the Missouri, two cities share one name: Kansas City, Missouri, and Kansas City, Kansas, with the state line running between them. The larger one is on the Missouri side. The city grew as a jumping-off point for the Santa Fe and Oregon trails, and later swung to its own style of jazz.
Q41819.w: Two rivers meeting at a sharp bend of the Missouri, with a downtown cluster on the bluffs just south-east of the confluence.
f: It calls itself the City of Fountains and has some 200 of them.
Count Basie's band and saxophonist Charlie Parker came out of Kansas City's 1930s jazz scene.
Covered wagons bound for the Santa Fe and Oregon trails outfitted in the towns here in the 1840s.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Kansas City?

Q16558.t: Where the West begins, as the city likes to say
Q16558.s: Fort Worth began in 1849 as an army outpost on the Trinity River and grew rich as a stop for cattle drives heading north on the Chisholm Trail. Its Stockyards still keep that cowboy spirit alive. Today it merges eastward with Dallas into one huge metro area; the giant DFW airport sits between the two.
Q16558.w: A city at the forks of the Trinity River, joined to Dallas by suburbs; the huge DFW airport with parallel runways halfway between.
f: Herds of longhorns passed through Fort Worth on the Chisholm Trail from the late 1860s.
DFW Airport, between Fort Worth and Dallas, covers more ground than Manhattan.
The Stockyards still stage a small cattle drive down the street twice a day.

q.q: What is Fort Worth's nickname?

Q6346.t: A planned capital with a racetrack you can spot
Q6346.s: Indianapolis was drawn on paper in 1821: a 'Mile Square' at the centre with four diagonal avenues cutting across the grid. It sits almost in the middle of flat, farmed Indiana, which is why it calls itself the Crossroads of America. North-west of downtown, a big oval stands out — the Speedway, home of the Indianapolis 500 since 1911.
Q6346.w: A city on flat farmland with motorways radiating like spokes; a large oval racetrack north-west of the centre.
f: The Indianapolis 500 has been raced at the Speedway since 1911.
The Speedway's oval is about 4 km around, big enough to pick out from cruise on a clear day.
The White River runs through the city from north to south-west.

q.q: Which famous race is held in Indianapolis every May?

Q49233.t: A city of round lakes and theme parks
Q49233.s: Count the lakes: Orlando is freckled with dozens of round blue ponds, many of them old sinkholes where the limestone below gave way. Until the late 1960s this was a quiet citrus town in central Florida. Then Walt Disney World opened south-west of the city in 1971, and Orlando became one of the most visited places on the planet.
Q49233.w: A city scattered with many small round lakes in flat central Florida; big theme-park complexes and resorts to the south-west.
f: Walt Disney World opened in 1971; it covers an area about the size of San Francisco.
Many of the region's round lakes formed as sinkholes in the limestone bedrock.
Kennedy Space Center lies about 80 km east, on the Atlantic coast.

q.q: What formed many of Orlando's round lakes?

Q26590.t: Half of a desert metropolis split by a river
Q26590.s: In the Chihuahuan Desert, a narrow river divides one large city between two countries: Ciudad Juárez in Mexico on the south bank, El Paso in Texas on the north. For centuries this was the 'pass of the north', a gap in the mountains on the royal road from Mexico City to Santa Fe. Factories making goods for export now ring the city.
Q26590.w: A large grid on the desert on the south bank of the Rio Grande, facing El Paso and the dark Franklin Mountains across the river.
f: Until 1888 the city was called El Paso del Norte; it was renamed after President Benito Juárez.
The mission of Our Lady of Guadalupe, founded in 1659, is the city's oldest building.
Together with El Paso it forms one of the largest cross-border urban areas in the world.

q.q: What was Ciudad Juárez called before 1888?

Q18383.t: A refuge for free thinkers at the head of a bay
Q18383.s: Narragansett Bay narrows northward to a point, and there sits Providence, the capital of tiny Rhode Island. Roger Williams founded it in 1636 after being expelled from Massachusetts for his beliefs, and he promised freedom of conscience to all. Later it grew rich on trade and jewellery making. Two small rivers meet in its compact downtown.
Q18383.w: The northern tip of a long bay with islands; a compact city at its head, and Boston about 80 km to the north-east.
f: Roger Williams named the settlement for God's 'merciful providence' in finding him a refuge.
Brown University, founded in 1764, is one of the oldest in the United States.
On summer evenings, WaterFire sets dozens of bonfires burning on the rivers downtown.

q.q: Who founded Providence in 1636?

Q16567.t: A capital planned on a riverbank, ringed by a beltway
Q16567.s: Look for a ring road drawn around a city on flat farmland, with two rivers meeting right at its heart: that is Columbus, the capital of Ohio. It was laid out in 1812 as a brand-new capital on the Scioto. Today it is the state's largest city, and its mix of residents mirrors America so closely that companies test new products here first.
Q16567.w: A compact downtown where two rivers meet, inside a round beltway, amid flat, square-cut Ohio farmland.
f: Columbus was chosen as Ohio's capital in 1812, when the site was little more than forest.
Fast-food chains and retailers often trial new products in Columbus because its population resembles the US average.
Ohio State University, on the Olentangy River, is one of the largest universities in the country.

q.q: Which two rivers meet in downtown Columbus, Ohio?

Q163749.t: The mainland town built to serve an island resort
Q163749.s: A narrow lagoon runs along Florida's coast here, and a skinny barrier island lies beyond it. The island is Palm Beach, where Henry Flagler built grand hotels in the 1890s; West Palm Beach, on the mainland, was laid out for the people who worked in them. Now the working town is the bigger city, and inland lies the vast Lake Okeechobee.
Q163749.w: A long lagoon between the mainland and a thin barrier island; far to the west, the huge round Lake Okeechobee.
f: Henry Flagler founded West Palm Beach in 1894 as a town for workers at his island resorts.
Lake Okeechobee, one of the largest freshwater lakes in the US, lies about 60 km west.
The Lake Worth Lagoon separates the city from the island of Palm Beach.

q.q: Which railway tycoon founded West Palm Beach?

ne-pp-1159148899.t: A quilombo village on a river in Brazil's far north
ne-pp-1159148899.s: This Vila Velha is not the big city in Espírito Santo but a small village of the same name, far to the north on the Cassiporé River in the state of Amapá. In 2016 it was recognised as a quilombo, a community descended from people who escaped slavery. Around it, forest gives way to wet grasslands and mangroves on the way to the Atlantic.
ne-pp-1159148899.w: A river winding through green forest and pale flooded grassland near the Atlantic coast, north of the Amazon's mouth.
f: The village belongs to the municipality of Oiapoque, which borders French Guiana.
At about 3° north, it lies only some 350 km from the equator.
The Cassiporé River runs from the forested interior of Amapá to the Atlantic.

q.q: In which Brazilian state is Vila Velha do Cassiporé?

Q334197.t: The old town facing the island capital
Q334197.s: The name means 'Old Town', and it's earned: founded in 1535, this is the oldest settlement in Espírito Santo. The colony's seat soon moved across the bay to the island of Vitória, but Vila Velha kept growing. Today it is the bigger of the two, a line of beaches and high-rises facing the ocean, with a convent crowning a granite hill.
Q334197.w: Long ocean beaches south of the bay mouth, facing the island city of Vitória; a steep granite hill near the water.
f: The Penha Convent, begun in the 16th century, sits on a granite hill above the bay.
The Garoto chocolate factory, one of Brazil's best-known brands, is in Vila Velha.
A tall bridge completed in 1989, the Terceira Ponte, links the city with Vitória.

q.q: What does the name Vila Velha mean?

Q52535.t: The flag's birthplace on a mighty brown river
Q52535.s: The Paraná here is a broad brown river, and beyond its main channel a maze of green islands and wetlands stretches for many kilometres. Rosario spreads along the western bank, and from its river ports much of Argentina's grain heads to sea. In 1812 General Manuel Belgrano first raised the country's blue-and-white flag on this riverbank. Lionel Messi grew up here.
Q52535.w: A large city on the west bank of a wide brown river; opposite, a maze of green islands crossed by a long straight causeway.
f: Manuel Belgrano first raised the Argentine flag on the bank of the Paraná here on 27 February 1812.
A bridge and a causeway about 60 km long cross the delta islands to the town of Victoria.
The river ports around Rosario ship a large part of Argentina's soybean harvest.

q.q: Which football star was born in Rosario?

Q168888.t: Turquoise reefs on one side, a lagoon on the other
Q168888.s: Maceió is squeezed between two waters: a big brown lagoon inland and a turquoise sea edged by reefs. At low tide, sail rafts called jangadas carry swimmers out to natural pools on the reef. Rows of coconut palms line the shore. The whole state, Alagoas, is named after its lagoons, and Maceió has been its capital since 1839.
Q168888.w: A coastal city between a large lagoon and the Atlantic; pale reef lines and turquoise water just offshore.
f: The state's name, Alagoas, means 'lagoons' in Portuguese.
Maceió took over as the capital of Alagoas in 1839.
The natural pools off Pajuçara beach are reached by jangada only at low tide.

q.q: What does the name of Maceió's state, Alagoas, mean?

Q16559.t: Hill Country meets prairie, and a million bats
Q16559.s: Austin sits right on a geological seam: to the west the wooded Hill Country, to the east flat prairie farmland. The Colorado River has been dammed into a chain of narrow lakes that wind through the hills. The capital of Texas calls itself the live-music capital of the world, and on summer evenings a cloud of bats spirals out from under a downtown bridge.
Q16559.w: A chain of narrow, winding lakes in wooded hills west of the city; flat farmland to the east.
f: Up to 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats roost under the Congress Avenue Bridge in summer.
The Balcones Escarpment, the edge between hills and plains, runs through the city.
The Texas Capitol in Austin stands a few metres taller than the US Capitol in Washington.

q.q: What colony lives under Austin's Congress Avenue Bridge?

Q386991.t: A green oasis on a riverbed that is usually dry
Q386991.s: In the middle of the northern Mexican desert, a large green patch of irrigated fields appears: La Laguna. Torreón is its biggest city, and across a mostly dry riverbed lie its twins, Gómez Palacio and Lerdo, in another state. It is a young city: a ranch with a watchtower became a railway junction and was declared a city only in 1907.
Q386991.w: A large city on pale desert at the foot of bare, rocky ridges, beside a green irrigated oasis and a wide, dry riverbed.
f: The name comes from the torreón, or watchtower, that stood on the original ranch.
Across the Nazas River, Gómez Palacio and Lerdo belong to the state of Durango, not Coahuila.
La Laguna's irrigated desert is one of Mexico's main dairy regions.

q.q: What gave Torreón its name?

Q79867.t: The Magic City, built on iron, coal and limestone
Q79867.s: Long wooded ridges run in parallel lines here, the southern end of the Appalachians, and Birmingham fills the valley between them. It was founded only in 1871, yet grew so fast it was nicknamed the Magic City. The reason lay in the ground: iron ore, coal and limestone, everything needed to make iron, were all within easy reach.
Q79867.w: A city in a long valley between parallel wooded ridges running south-west to north-east.
f: Red Mountain, the ridge south of downtown, is named for the iron ore once mined in it.
A statue of Vulcan on Red Mountain is the largest cast-iron statue in the world.
Birmingham is the most populous metro area in Alabama.

q.q: What is Birmingham, Alabama, nicknamed?

Q4709.t: A city of music and a sea of pilgrims
Q4709.s: On a dry plateau above the green valley of the Turbio River, Barquisimeto spreads out in long, straight avenues. Around it, the hills are scrubby and full of cacti. Venezuelans call it their musical capital. Every 14 January the city fills with an enormous crowd following the image of the Divina Pastora, one of the largest religious processions in the Americas.
Q4709.w: A large, regular grid on a plateau above a green river valley, surrounded by dry, brownish hills.
f: The Divina Pastora procession carries the image from the town of Santa Rosa to the cathedral.
The city was founded in the 1550s by Spanish settlers and moved more than once before settling here.
Lara state is the home of the tamunangue, a cycle of folk dances in honour of St Anthony.

q.q: What is Barquisimeto often called?

Q210307.t: A giant grid on a vanished lake
Q210307.s: Right beside Mexico City's airport runways lies an astonishingly regular grid of streets, packed tight with houses. That is Ciudad Nezahualcóyotl, built on the dried-out bed of Lake Texcoco. As the lake shrank in the 20th century, settlers flocked to the new land, and within a few decades it had over a million people. Its name honours a poet-king.
Q210307.w: A dense, rectangular street grid immediately east of Mexico City airport; the flat, pale remains of Lake Texcoco to the north-east.
f: The city is named after Nezahualcóyotl, the 15th-century poet-king of Texcoco.
Every street stands on land that was the bed of Lake Texcoco.
It became a separate municipality only in 1963.

q.q: Who was Nezahualcóyotl, the city's namesake?

Q131620.t: Born on Christmas Day, surrounded by dunes
Q131620.s: Near the north-eastern corner of Brazil, where the coast turns, white dunes pile up beside the sea and a river snakes into the Atlantic. Natal sits between them. The name means 'Christmas': the city was founded on 25 December 1599. At the river mouth, a star-shaped Portuguese fort still stands on the reef.
Q131620.w: A coastal city between a winding river mouth and bright white dunes, near the corner where Brazil's coast turns west.
f: The Forte dos Reis Magos, begun in 1598, guards the mouth of the Potengi River.
Just south of the city, a single cashew tree at Pirangi spreads over some 8,500 m².
Dune buggies race over the Genipabu dunes, just north of the city.

q.q: What does the city name Natal mean?

Q49261.t: Desert fields watered by thousand-year-old canals
Q49261.s: East of Phoenix, the Valley of the Sun becomes one immense grid of streets, and Mesa is its eastern anchor. Mormon settlers founded it in 1878 and reopened canals first dug by the Hohokam people many centuries before. Beyond the last suburbs, the jagged Superstition Mountains rise out of the desert.
Q49261.w: An endless street grid in the desert east of Phoenix; the Salt River's pale bed to the north, jagged mountains to the east.
f: The Hohokam dug hundreds of kilometres of irrigation canals here long before Europeans arrived.
Mesa is the third-largest city in Arizona, after Phoenix and Tucson.
The Superstition Mountains are said to hide the legendary Lost Dutchman's gold mine.

q.q: Which ancient people dug the canals that Mesa's settlers reused?

Q28441.t: The island capital the French founded
Q28441.s: On Brazil's north coast a wide, muddy bay holds a large island, and on its north-western corner sits São Luís. The French founded it in 1612, the only Brazilian state capital with that origin, though the Portuguese took it within a few years. The tides here are among the biggest in Brazil, laying bare broad mudflats twice a day.
Q28441.w: A large island in a broad, silty bay on the northern coast; wide tidal flats and river mouths around it.
f: The old town, with its tiled colonial facades, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997.
Tides in São Marcos Bay can rise and fall by about 7 m.
The city is named after King Louis XIII of France.

q.q: Which European nation founded São Luís in 1612?

Q49174.t: The showman's city on Long Island Sound
Q49174.s: Connecticut's biggest city faces Long Island across a broad sound, with ferries crossing the water between them. In the 19th century Bridgeport was a factory town of sewing machines, corsets and brass, and home to the showman P. T. Barnum, who wintered his circus here and even served as mayor. Its harbour sits at the mouth of a small river.
Q49174.w: A city on the north shore of Long Island Sound, about 90 km north-east of Manhattan; Long Island visible across the water.
f: P. T. Barnum was elected mayor of Bridgeport in 1875.
General Tom Thumb, Barnum's famous small performer, was born here in 1838.
A car ferry runs from Bridgeport across the Sound to Port Jefferson on Long Island.

q.q: Which famous showman was once mayor of Bridgeport?

Q243766.t: A city of parks perched on a plateau
Q243766.s: Bucaramanga sits on a flat-topped shelf in the eastern Andes, and its western edge breaks off in steep, eroded slopes. It is known as the City of Parks for its many green squares. To the south-west, the Chicamocha River has carved a spectacular canyon. Locals snack on roasted big-bottomed ants, a Santander speciality.
Q243766.w: A city on a flat plateau whose edge drops in eroded slopes; higher Andean ridges to the east, a deep canyon to the south-west.
f: Roasted hormigas culonas — 'big-bottomed ants' — are a traditional snack of the Santander region.
A cable car in Chicamocha National Park crosses the canyon from rim to river and up the far side.
The city lies at about 1,000 m, so its climate is warm but not stifling.

q.q: What is Bucaramanga's nickname?

Q333928.t: The garden city between the mountains and a lake
Q333928.s: North of Maracay, the coastal mountains are clothed in cloud forest; to the south-west spreads Lake Valencia, which has no outlet to the sea. The city fills the green valley between them. Its tree-lined avenues earned it the name Garden City. The forest above became Henri Pittier National Park, Venezuela's first, in 1937.
Q333928.w: A city in a green valley between forested coastal mountains and a large lake to its south-west.
f: Henri Pittier National Park was created in 1937 as Venezuela's first national park.
Lake Valencia has no natural outlet: its rivers flow in, but none flows out.
The park's Portachuelo Pass is a famous crossing point for migrating birds.

q.q: What is special about Lake Valencia near Maracay?
q.a: It has no outlet to the sea

Q183124.t: A valley of eternal spring, watched by a giant Christ
Q183124.s: In the Bolivian Andes, a broad green valley opens between bare brown mountains, and Cochabamba fills its floor. At about 2,500 m, the climate is mild all year, so it is called the City of Eternal Spring. On a hill at the city's edge stands a statue of Christ with open arms, a little taller than the one in Rio.
Q183124.w: A green, cultivated valley floor ringed by bare mountains; a higher, often snow-dusted range along the north side.
f: The Cristo de la Concordia, completed in 1994, is taller than Rio de Janeiro's Christ the Redeemer.
The Tunari range north of the city rises above 5,000 m.
The valley's farms have long made Cochabamba one of Bolivia's breadbaskets.

q.q: What is Cochabamba's nickname?

Q204271.t: Named in hope of silver riches
Q204271.s: When gold and silver were found in the hills nearby in 1592, the Spanish added 'Potosí' to this city's name, hoping it would rival the fabled silver mountain in Bolivia. It never quite did, but it prospered. San Luis Potosí sits at about 1,860 m on a dry plateau of scrub and cactus, and its colonial core is full of pink stone.
Q204271.w: A large city on a high, dry plateau; rugged mountains to the south-west, pale scrubland in every direction.
f: Gold and silver were found at Cerro de San Pedro, just east of the city, in 1592.
Its historic centre is part of the UNESCO-listed Camino Real de Tierra Adentro.
The city is the capital of the state of the same name in north-central Mexico.

q.q: Which famous mining town inspired the name San Luis Potosí?

Q16568.t: The biggest city in the lower 48 — by area
Q16568.s: Jacksonville covers more land than any other city in the contiguous United States, sprawling over forests, marshes and suburbs. Through the middle runs the broad St. Johns River, which flows north for most of its length before turning east to the Atlantic. In 1564 French Huguenots built Fort Caroline near its mouth, decades before the first English colony.
Q16568.w: A wide, dark river curving north then east through the city to the sea, crossed by several bridges; forests and marsh all around.
f: By land area, Jacksonville is the largest city in the contiguous United States.
The St. Johns River flows north for most of its roughly 500 km.
Fort Caroline, founded in 1564, was one of the first European settlements in what is now the US.

q.q: Which way does Jacksonville's St. Johns River mainly flow?

Q44989.t: An oil boomtown on the sandy Arkansas River
Q44989.s: In 1905 a gusher at Glenn Pool, just south of town, changed everything: within a few years Tulsa was calling itself the Oil Capital of the World. The money built a downtown full of Art Deco towers. The city stretches along the broad, sandy Arkansas River, where green prairie meets the wooded hills of north-eastern Oklahoma.
Q44989.w: A city on a wide, sandy river with pale sandbars; wooded hills to the north-west and a large reservoir to the west.
f: Oil from the Glenn Pool field, struck in 1905, turned Tulsa into a boomtown.
Cyrus Avery of Tulsa, called the 'Father of Route 66', helped plan the highway, which runs through the city.
The name comes from Tallasi, the old town of the Creek people who settled here in 1836.

q.q: What did Tulsa call itself during its early 1900s boom?

Q43421.t: Whitewater rapids right below the capital's towers
Q43421.s: Few capitals have whitewater downtown, but Richmond does: here the James River tumbles over the fall line in rocky, braided rapids between wooded islands. The city grew at this spot because ships from the sea could go no farther. In 1775 Patrick Henry cried 'Give me liberty, or give me death!' in one of its churches; five years later Richmond became Virginia's capital.
Q43421.w: A river breaking into rocky rapids and islands just below the downtown towers, where the hills meet the flat coastal plain.
f: Two US presidents, James Monroe and John Tyler, are buried in Hollywood Cemetery on the river bluffs.
Thomas Jefferson designed the Virginia State Capitol, modelled on a Roman temple in Nîmes.
The James River drops about 30 m through the city over a stretch of roughly 10 km.

q.q: Which river tumbles over rapids in downtown Richmond?

Q165341.t: The north-eastern capital that turned its back on the sea
Q165341.s: Every other state capital in north-east Brazil sits on the coast; Teresina alone lies inland, in the fork between two rivers, the Parnaíba and the Poti. It was planned from scratch in 1852 and named after Empress Teresa Cristina. It is one of the hottest cities in the country, and its many trees earned it the name Green City.
Q165341.w: A city in the fork of two winding rivers on a flat plain, with another town across the larger river to the west.
f: Teresina was built in 1852 to replace the old capital, Oeiras, and to be closer to the river trade.
The Parnaíba River divides it from the neighbouring state of Maranhão.
The empress it honours was the wife of Emperor Pedro II.

q.q: Whom is Teresina named after?

Q34804.t: Watermelon mountains and a sky full of balloons
Q34804.s: At sunset the long ridge east of Albuquerque glows pink, which may be why the Spanish called it Sandía, 'watermelon'. The city spreads over high desert mesas at about 1,500 m, cut by a green ribbon of cottonwoods along the Rio Grande. Each October hundreds of hot-air balloons lift off together at the International Balloon Fiesta.
Q34804.w: A green river ribbon through a sprawling desert city; a steep mountain wall to the east, small dark volcanic cones to the west.
f: The Balloon Fiesta, held every October, is the largest hot-air balloon festival in the world.
Founded in 1706, the town was named after the Duke of Alburquerque, then viceroy of New Spain.
On the West Mesa, a line of small volcanoes overlooks thousands of ancient petroglyphs.

q.q: What does 'Sandía', in the Sandia Mountains, mean in Spanish?

Q199440.t: Green fields end at a line: the border and the desert
Q199440.s: Here the desert is cut into a vivid green checkerboard by water from the Colorado River, and a razor-straight line runs across it: the border between Mexico and the United States. Mexicali, capital of Baja California, lies right against it, facing the smaller Calexico. The two names are mirror images, blending 'Mexico' and 'California' in opposite order.
Q199440.w: A city on a straight border line, in a checkerboard of irrigated fields that ends abruptly at bare desert and mountains to the west.
f: Chinese workers who came to farm cotton in the early 1900s made Chinese food a local staple.
The Cerro Prieto geothermal field south of the city is one of the largest in the world.
Summer temperatures here regularly climb above 40 °C.

q.q: Which US town faces Mexicali across the border?

Q44255.s: On 9 July 1816, in a colonial house in this city, delegates declared the independence of the United Provinces of South America — today's Argentina. Tucumán lies on a green plain at the foot of a steep, forested mountain wall. Its province is the smallest in Argentina, and so fertile with sugar cane and lemons that it is called the Garden of the Republic.
Q44255.w: A large city on a green plain, with a forested mountain wall rising sharply to the west; cane fields all around.
f: Argentina's Independence Day, 9 July, commemorates the declaration signed here in 1816.
Tucumán province is one of the world's leading producers of lemons.
Behind the city, the Sierra de San Javier and higher Aconquija ranges catch the rain that feeds its forests.

q.q: What was declared in Tucumán on 9 July 1816?

Q18575.t: A desert city guarded by giant cacti
Q18575.s: Tucson spreads across a desert basin ringed by mountains, and on both its east and west sides lie the two halves of Saguaro National Park, a forest of giant cacti. North of the city the Santa Catalina Mountains rise steeply, often with snow on top in winter. The city began as a Spanish fort in 1775.
Q18575.w: A pale street grid in a desert basin; steep mountains close to the north, others to the east and west.
f: In 2015 Tucson became the first UNESCO City of Gastronomy in the United States.
Mount Lemmon, in the Santa Catalinas, rises to about 2,790 m.
The white Mission San Xavier del Bac, south of the city, was completed in 1797.

q.q: Which giant cactus gives Tucson's national park its name?

Q159273.t: A white city beneath three great volcanoes
Q159273.s: Three giant volcanoes stand over Arequipa, and the nearest, El Misti, is an almost perfect cone of 5,822 m. The city lies in a green valley in the desert at about 2,300 m, and its colonial centre is built of sillar, a white volcanic stone — hence the nickname the White City. Even from cruise height, Misti's cone is unmistakable.
Q159273.w: A green valley in brown desert; right above it a symmetrical cone, a broader massif to its north-west and a jagged ridge to its south-east.
f: The historic centre, built of white sillar, has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2000.
Chachani, the broad massif beside Misti, rises to about 6,050 m.
The Colca Canyon, north of Arequipa, is more than twice as deep as the Grand Canyon.

q.q: What is Arequipa's old town built from?

Q211760.t: Two rivers become one in a farming heartland
Q211760.s: Culiacán grew where two rivers from the Sierra Madre, the Tamazula and the Humaya, join to form the Culiacán River. Around the city, a green checkerboard of irrigated fields stretches toward the Gulf of California. Those fields send tomatoes and other vegetables north across the border all winter. Founded in 1531, it is one of the oldest Spanish towns in north-western Mexico.
Q211760.w: A city where two rivers merge, on a green coastal plain of irrigated fields; forested Sierra Madre foothills to the east.
f: The Tamazula and Humaya rivers meet in the heart of the city.
San Miguel de Culiacán was founded in 1531 by the conquistador Nuño de Guzmán.
Culiacán is the capital of the state of Sinaloa.

q.q: Which two rivers join at Culiacán?

Q170762.t: The very centre of South America
Q170762.s: Cuiabá claims the heart of the continent: a monument in the city marks the geodesic centre of South America. The capital of Mato Grosso grew from a gold rush in 1719 on the winding Cuiabá River. To the south stretch the flat wetlands of the Pantanal; to the north-east rise the red sandstone cliffs of the Chapada dos Guimarães. It is famously, fiercely hot.
Q170762.w: A city on a flat plain, split by a winding river; red cliffs of a plateau to the north-east, low wetlands to the south.
f: The centre of South America was calculated by Marshal Rondon's survey in 1909 and marked in Cuiabá.
Gold found in the river in 1719 brought the first settlers.
Afternoon temperatures in the dry season often pass 40 °C.

q.q: What is Cuiabá said to mark?

Q49218.t: A waterfall downtown and the birthplace of Kodak
Q49218.s: The Genesee River flows north through Rochester to Lake Ontario, and right in the city centre it drops over a waterfall nearly 30 m high. Those falls powered the mills that first made the town. Later, George Eastman founded Kodak here, and the Kodak camera went on sale in 1888. Every May, the city's lilac festival lives up to its nickname, the Flower City.
Q49218.w: A city on the south shore of Lake Ontario, with a river running north through it into the lake.
f: George Eastman's Kodak camera, sold loaded with film, went on sale in 1888.
The original Erie Canal crossed the Genesee River in Rochester on a stone aqueduct.
Suffragist Susan B. Anthony lived in Rochester for four decades.

q.q: Which photography company was founded in Rochester?

Q16562.t: A Texas city split by a mountain range
Q16562.s: A bare, rocky mountain range runs right into the heart of El Paso, dividing the city into east and west. At its southern tip, the Rio Grande separates El Paso from Ciudad Juárez, and the two cities blend into one big desert metropolis. El Paso is so far west that, unlike almost all of Texas, it keeps Mountain Time.
Q16562.w: A dark mountain ridge pushing into a desert city from the north; a thin river and the border along its south side.
f: El Paso keeps Mountain Time, an hour behind Dallas and Houston.
Franklin Mountains State Park, inside the city limits, is one of the largest urban parks in the US.
Spanish travellers called this gap between mountains El Paso del Norte, 'the pass of the north'.

q.q: Which time zone does El Paso use?

Q28848.t: The other Twin City, once called Pig's Eye
Q28848.s: Where the Mississippi swings through a deep valley between limestone bluffs, Saint Paul sits on the east, and Minneapolis's towers rise a few kilometres to the west. Together they are the Twin Cities. Saint Paul is Minnesota's capital, yet its first settlement bore a less dignified name: Pig's Eye, after a local tavern keeper.
Q28848.w: A city on the bluffs of a winding Mississippi, with Minneapolis's taller towers just to the west and lakes all around.
f: The settlement was renamed after a log chapel dedicated to St Paul, built in 1841.
F. Scott Fitzgerald was born in Saint Paul in 1896.
The Saint Paul Winter Carnival has been held on and off since 1886.

q.q: What was Saint Paul's early nickname?

Q128069.t: Salt City, where the lake snow never quits
Q128069.s: Syracuse sits at the south end of little Onondaga Lake, whose salt springs gave the city its first fortune and its nickname, Salt City. The Erie Canal once ran right through downtown. In winter, cold air picking up moisture over Lake Ontario dumps so much snow here that Syracuse is regularly among the snowiest large cities in the United States.
Q128069.w: A city at the southern tip of a small lake; the long, narrow Finger Lakes to the south-west, Lake Ontario to the north-west.
f: Salt from Onondaga Lake's springs once supplied much of the United States.
The old route of the Erie Canal through downtown is now Erie Boulevard.
The city was named after Syracuse in Sicily, which also had salt springs nearby.

q.q: Where does Syracuse, New York, get its name?

Q185582.s: Two rivers flowing out of the mountains, the Holston and the French Broad, meet just east of Knoxville, and from there the water is called the Tennessee River. The city fills a long Appalachian valley, with the blue wall of the Great Smoky Mountains on the south-eastern horizon. Knoxville was Tennessee's first capital, in 1796.
Q185582.w: A river city in a long valley between wooded ridges; the high, blue-grey Smoky Mountains to the south-east.
f: The Tennessee River officially begins at Knoxville and flows about 1,050 km to the Ohio.
Great Smoky Mountains National Park, the most visited in the US, lies about 50 km to the south-east.
The city hosted the World's Fair in 1982.

q.q: Which river begins at Knoxville?

Q43301.t: In the middle of America's great garden valley
Q43301.s: Fresno sits right in the middle of the San Joaquin Valley, a flat patchwork of orchards and vineyards that is one of the most productive farming regions on Earth. Most of America's raisins are dried in the vineyards around it. To the east the Sierra Nevada rises abruptly, snowy in winter, hiding Yosemite and the giant sequoias.
Q43301.w: A large flat grid amid a vast patchwork of orchards and vineyards; the wall of the Sierra Nevada rising to the east.
f: Fresno is Spanish for 'ash tree', after the trees that grew along the San Joaquin River.
Yosemite, Kings Canyon and Sequoia national parks are all within a couple of hours' drive.
Nearly all of America's raisins come from the San Joaquin Valley, much of it around Fresno.

q.q: What does 'Fresno' mean in Spanish?

Q189138.t: A desert capital around a lonely hill
Q189138.s: Hermosillo sprawls across the flat Sonoran Desert, with a lone rocky hill, the Cerro de la Campana, rising near its centre. Summers here are fierce, with temperatures that can pass 45 °C. The capital of Sonora is known for beef, carne asada and enormous, paper-thin flour tortillas. About 100 km west, the desert meets the Gulf of California.
Q189138.w: A city on flat brown desert with a single rocky hill near its centre; a reservoir to the east, bare ranges around.
f: The city is named after José María González de Hermosillo, a fighter in Mexico's independence war.
Kino Bay, on the Gulf of California, lies about 100 km to the west.
Sonora is famous for its huge, thin flour tortillas, often wider than a dinner plate.

q.q: Which sea lies about 100 km west of Hermosillo?

Q334577.t: A highland city beside a steaming volcano
Q334577.s: Quetzaltenango, which everyone calls Xela, sits in a high valley at about 2,300 m, and its skyline is volcanoes. Just to the south rises the tall cone of Santa María, and on its flank a younger lava dome, Santiaguito, has been active since 1922 and often puffs out ash and steam. Guatemala's second city is cool, stony and full of Spanish-language students.
Q334577.w: A city in a high basin; to the south a tall volcanic cone, often with a plume of steam or ash on its flank.
f: Xela is short for Xelajú, the city's name in the K'iche' Maya language.
The Santa María volcano, about 3,770 m, rises just south of the city.
Santiaguito, a lava dome on Santa María's side, has been growing since 1922.

q.q: What do locals call Quetzaltenango?

Q194328.t: A farming hub on the red plateau of the cerrado
Q194328.s: Look for huge rectangular fields and green circles of centre-pivot irrigation stretching to the horizon: that is the Triângulo Mineiro, the western wedge of Minas Gerais, and Uberlândia is its biggest city. It grew up as a crossroads for grain, trucks and warehouses on the high cerrado plateau. Until 1929 it was called São Pedro de Uberabinha.
Q194328.w: A large city on flat farmland of vast rectangular fields and irrigation circles; reservoirs on the rivers around.
f: The city took the name Uberlândia in 1929.
The name mixes Latin 'uber', fertile, with 'land'.
The Triângulo Mineiro lies between two big rivers, the Grande and the Paranaíba.

q.q: What was Uberlândia called before 1929?

Q188901.s: For more than a century, drovers brought great herds of mules up from southern Brazil to Sorocaba's annual fair, and from here the animals carried goods all over the country. Later, textile mills earned the city the nickname Manchester of São Paulo. Today it is a big industrial city on rolling hills about 90 km west of São Paulo.
Q188901.w: A sizeable city on rolling green hills west of São Paulo, with a long reservoir to its south-east.
f: Sorocaba was founded in 1654.
Its mule fair was the biggest in Brazil through much of the 18th and 19th centuries.
One of Brazil's first ironworks, the Ipanema foundry, opened nearby in the early 1800s.

q.q: What was Sorocaba nicknamed for its textile mills?

Q117040.t: A pocket bay behind a castle, under Cuba's highest mountains
Q117040.s: Santiago de Cuba hides behind a narrow gap in the cliffs: the bay opens up only once you are through it, and the city climbs the hills around its inner shore. A stone castle has guarded that entrance since the 17th century. Westward rise the dark ridges of the Sierra Maestra. This is the city of son, the music that grew into salsa.
Q117040.w: A pouch-shaped bay behind a narrow entrance on Cuba's south-east coast; the city on hills around it, dark mountains to the west.
f: The Castillo de San Pedro de la Roca at the bay mouth has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997.
Pico Turquino, Cuba's highest peak at about 1,970 m, rises in the Sierra Maestra west of the city.
Diego Velázquez founded Santiago in 1515, making it one of Cuba's oldest cities.

q.q: Which mountain range rises west of Santiago de Cuba?

Q188892.t: Coffee capital turned ocean of sugar cane
Q188892.s: Around Ribeirão Preto the land is a sea of sugar cane cut into huge rectangles, and where a field is bare, the soil shows a deep purplish red. That rich 'terra roxa' once made this the heart of Brazil's coffee empire. Today cane and ethanol rule, and the city is so prosperous that it's been called the Brazilian California.
Q188892.w: A large city in an endless patchwork of cane fields, with patches of dark-red bare soil, in the north of São Paulo state.
f: Ribeirão Preto means 'black stream'.
Around 1900 its plantations made it known as the world capital of coffee.
Each year the city hosts Agrishow, one of Latin America's largest farm-machinery fairs.

q.q: What does the name Ribeirão Preto mean?

Q738353.t: The last border city before the river meets the Gulf
Q738353.s: The Rio Grande makes its final loops through flat delta land here, and Matamoros sits on the south bank, facing Brownsville in Texas. A few dozen kilometres east, the river slips into the Gulf of Mexico. Around the city stretch shallow lagoons and marsh. It takes its name from Mariano Matamoros, a priest who fought for Mexico's independence.
Q738353.w: Twin cities on the last big loops of the Rio Grande; flat delta and shallow lagoons between them and the Gulf coast.
f: The city is named after Mariano Matamoros, a priest and hero of Mexico's independence war.
The Rio Grande reaches the Gulf of Mexico some 35 km east of the city.
The Laguna Madre along the coast is one of the few hypersaline lagoons in the world.

q.q: Which Texan city faces Matamoros across the Rio Grande?

Q131429.t: A green-stone city watched by a flattened mountaintop
Q131429.s: Three valleys meet in the mountains of southern Mexico, and Oaxaca lies where they join, at about 1,550 m. More than 2,000 years ago the Zapotecs levelled the top of a ridge above the valley and built a city there, Monte Albán. Below, the colonial town grew in pale green stone. Today it is known for its markets, mezcal and seven kinds of mole.
Q131429.w: A city where three valley arms meet, ringed by mountains; a long ridge rising just west of the centre.
f: The historic centre and Monte Albán have been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1987.
The Tule tree, a cypress in a village just east of the city, has one of the thickest trunks in the world.
Every July the Guelaguetza festival gathers dancers from all the state's regions.

q.q: Which people built Monte Albán above Oaxaca?

Q234053.t: The older Vancouver, across the river from Portland
Q234053.s: Not the Canadian one: this Vancouver sits on the north bank of the broad Columbia River in Washington State, facing Portland, Oregon. It is actually the older of the two. In 1825 the Hudson's Bay Company built Fort Vancouver here as the hub of its fur trade in the Pacific Northwest. On a clear day, Mount Hood and Mount St. Helens stand on the horizon.
Q234053.w: A city on the north bank of a wide river, opposite Portland; snowy Mount Hood to the east, Mount St. Helens to the north-east.
f: Fort Vancouver, built in 1825, was the Hudson's Bay Company's headquarters on the Pacific coast.
The Canadian city of Vancouver was incorporated only in 1886.
Both cities are named after George Vancouver, the British captain who charted this coast in the 1790s.

q.q: Which city faces Vancouver, Washington, across the Columbia River?

Q36307.t: Salta the Beautiful, gateway to the high Andes
Q36307.s: Argentines call it Salta la Linda, 'Salta the Beautiful', for its colonial arcades and churches. The city fills a green valley at about 1,150 m, ringed by forested hills, with the bare, high Andes rising beyond. From here the Train to the Clouds climbs to a viaduct above 4,000 m, and roads lead to red canyons and high-altitude vineyards.
Q36307.w: A city on a green valley floor ringed by wooded hills; higher, bare Andean ranges to the west.
f: Salta was founded in 1582 by Hernando de Lerma, who gave his name to the valley.
The Train to the Clouds reaches the La Polvorilla viaduct at about 4,200 m.
Vineyards in the province, some above 2,000 m, are famous for the white Torrontés wine.

q.q: What is Salta's famous mountain railway called?
x: The Train at the End of the World

Q49258.t: The mountain that inspired 'America the Beautiful'
Q49258.s: The Great Plains run west as flat as a table until they hit a wall of mountains, and Colorado Springs sits right at the join. Above it looms Pikes Peak, 4,302 m high and often white with snow. In 1893 the view from its summit moved Katharine Lee Bates to write the words of 'America the Beautiful'. Red sandstone fins stand at the city's western edge.
Q49258.w: A city where the flat plains meet the Rockies, with the massive, often snowy bulk of Pikes Peak directly to the west.
f: Pikes Peak rises more than 2,400 m above the city.
The red rock fins of the Garden of the Gods are a free public park on the city's west side.
The US Olympic and Paralympic Training Center is based in Colorado Springs.

q.q: Which song was inspired by the view from Pikes Peak?

Q44244.t: A capital between lagoons on the Paraná floodplain
Q44244.s: Santa Fe sits on a strip of land between lagoons and river channels, on the wide, watery floodplain of the Paraná. Across the water, on a high bank, stands its sister city, Paraná, linked by a tunnel under the river. In 1853 Argentina's constitution was adopted here. The city's emblem is the Puente Colgante, a suspension bridge over the lagoon.
Q44244.w: A city between lagoons and river channels on a wide, green floodplain; another city on the high bank opposite.
f: Argentina's national constitution was adopted in Santa Fe in 1853.
Juan de Garay founded the city in 1573; it moved to its present site in the 1650s.
The Hernandarias tunnel, opened in 1969, carries traffic beneath the Paraná River.

q.q: Which city faces Santa Fe across the river, linked by a tunnel?

Q193289.t: The big city no road can reach
Q193289.s: Iquitos is surrounded by rainforest in every direction, and no highway leads to it: you arrive by plane or by boat. It is often called the largest city in the world that cannot be reached by road. The Amazon flows past its edge, joined by two smaller rivers, and in the Belén district houses stand on stilts or float with the seasonal flood.
Q193289.w: A city on a bend of a huge brown river, hemmed in by smaller rivers and oxbow lakes, with unbroken forest all around.
f: About 100 km upstream, the Marañón and Ucayali rivers join to form the Amazon.
The rubber boom of the late 1800s filled the city with mansions faced with European tiles.
In the rainy season the river can rise by several metres, lifting Belén's floating houses.

q.q: How do most people travel to Iquitos?

Q44241.t: A vineyard oasis in a sun-baked Andean valley
Q44241.s: In the rain shadow of the Andes, San Juan is a green island of vineyards and poplar windbreaks in a brown desert valley, watered by the San Juan River. The province is Argentina's second-biggest wine producer. The sun shines here almost every day. San Juan is also the birthplace of Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, the president who spread public schools across Argentina.
Q44241.w: A green oasis of vineyards in a brown desert valley; a reservoir to the west, bare Andean foothills beyond.
f: Domingo Faustino Sarmiento was born in San Juan in 1811.
San Juan is Argentina's second-largest wine province, after Mendoza.
Ischigualasto, in the north of the province, holds some of the oldest known dinosaur fossils.

q.q: Which Argentine president was born in San Juan?

Q16868.t: America's busy trade gateway on the Rio Grande
Q16868.s: Look for lorries: long lines of them crawl over the bridges at Laredo, one of the busiest trade crossings between the United States and Mexico. The city sits on the north bank of the Rio Grande in Texas, facing Nuevo Laredo. It was founded in 1755 as a Spanish ranching town, and for a few months in 1840 it was the capital of a would-be republic.
Q16868.w: Twin cities across a looping river in flat, dry brush country; big bridges and rail yards on both banks.
f: Laredo was founded in 1755 by Tomás Sánchez as a settlement of New Spain.
In 1840 it was the capital of the short-lived Republic of the Rio Grande.
The city's Washington's Birthday Celebration, held since 1898, is the largest in the US.

q.q: Which Mexican city faces Laredo across the Rio Grande?

Q28218.t: A red stick on the banks of the Mississippi
Q28218.s: In 1699 French explorers paddling up the Mississippi saw a red-painted pole on the bluff here, marking a hunting boundary between two tribes. They called the spot Baton Rouge, 'red stick'. Today it is Louisiana's capital, with refineries and docks lining the river. It is as far up the Mississippi as big ocean-going ships can sail.
Q28218.w: A city on the east bank of the broad, winding Mississippi; docks and industry along the river, swamps and oxbow lakes around.
f: The name means 'red stick', after the painted pole the French saw in 1699.
Louisiana's State Capitol, about 137 m tall, is the tallest state capitol in the US.
Louisiana State University's campus lies south of downtown, by the river.

q.q: What does 'Baton Rouge' mean?

Q468782.t: A high Andean valley of farms, fairs and railways
Q468782.s: At about 3,250 m, the Mantaro Valley opens wide and flat between the ranges of the central Peruvian Andes, a patchwork of potato and maize fields. Huancayo is its busy market capital. A railway climbs here from Lima over one of the highest passes in the world. On clear days, the snowy peaks of the Huaytapallana range shine to the north-east.
Q468782.w: A broad, flat valley floor high in the Andes, a braided river along it; snowy peaks to the north-east.
f: The Central Railway from Lima to Huancayo crosses the Andes at more than 4,700 m.
The Mantaro River leaves the valley through deep gorges and eventually joins the Apurímac.
Huancayo's Sunday market spreads for blocks along one of its main avenues.

q.q: Which valley is Huancayo the main city of?

Q38453.t: A planned capital where two rivers become one
Q38453.s: Columbia was one of the first planned cities in America: in 1786 South Carolina's lawmakers laid out a new capital in the middle of the state. The Broad and Saluda rivers meet here to form the Congaree. Just south-east lies Congaree National Park, a dark, swampy old-growth forest, and to the west spreads the branching blue of Lake Murray.
Q38453.w: A city at a river confluence, with a large branching lake to the west and dark floodplain forest to the south-east.
f: Columbia was laid out in 1786 to replace Charleston as the capital.
Congaree National Park protects the largest old-growth bottomland hardwood forest left in the south-eastern US.
Lake Murray was created by a dam on the Saluda River completed in 1930.

q.q: Which two rivers meet at Columbia to form the Congaree?
x: The Broad and the Pee Dee

Q223966.t: Peru's first Spanish city, in the sun-baked north
Q223966.s: In 1532, before he marched inland to meet the Inca, Francisco Pizarro founded a town in this northern desert: Piura, the first Spanish city in Peru. It moved a few times before settling on the river. Around it spreads the pale Sechura Desert, dotted with dry algarrobo forest. Its residents call it the City of Eternal Heat.
Q223966.w: A city on a river in flat, pale desert near the Pacific coast, with green irrigated strips along the water.
f: Piura was founded in 1532 as San Miguel de Piura.
The algarrobo, a kind of mesquite, is the tree of the northern Peruvian desert and a local emblem.
In strong El Niño years, heavy rains can briefly fill the Sechura Desert with lakes.

q.q: Who founded Piura in 1532?

Q320015.t: A carnival city at the foot of a volcano
Q320015.s: Pasto lies in a high green valley of the southern Colombian Andes at about 2,500 m, and the Galeras volcano rises right at its western edge. Every January the city explodes into the Carnival of Blacks and Whites, when people paint each other's faces and giant floats parade through the streets. To the south-east lies the large mountain lake of La Cocha.
Q320015.w: A city in a high green valley with a large volcano rising at its western edge; a big lake to the south-east.
f: The Carnival of Blacks and Whites has been on UNESCO's intangible heritage list since 2009.
Galeras volcano rises to about 4,280 m, more than 1,700 m above the city.
Barniz de Pasto, a lacquer made from the resin of the mopa-mopa shrub, is a centuries-old local craft.

q.q: Which carnival is Pasto famous for?
q.a: The Carnival of Blacks and Whites

Q110017.t: Italian vineyards in Brazil's southern highlands
Q110017.s: In 1875 families from the Veneto began clearing the araucaria forest on these high, hilly lands of southern Brazil, and they brought their vines with them. Caxias do Sul grew from those colonies into an industrial city, but grapes still define it. Every few years the Festa da Uva celebrates the harvest. Winters here are cold, and snow is not unknown.
Q110017.w: A city on high, hilly ground with dark araucaria woods and vineyards; deep river valleys cutting into the plateau.
f: Italian immigrants, mostly from the Veneto, began settling the area in 1875.
The Festa da Uva, a grape festival, was first held in 1931.
Marcopolo, one of the world's big bus-body makers, is based in Caxias do Sul.

q.q: Where did most of Caxias do Sul's first settlers come from?

Q235190.t: A city balanced on a knife-edge ridge
Q235190.s: Manizales was built along the crest of a narrow Andean ridge, so its streets run along the top and the slopes fall away steeply on both sides. Settlers from Antioquia founded it in 1849, in the heart of coffee country. On clear mornings, the snowy summit of the Nevado del Ruiz shines to the south-east. Cable cars serve as public transport here.
Q235190.w: A city strung along a narrow ridge with steep green slopes on both sides; a snow-capped volcano to the south-east.
f: Manizales was founded in 1849 by settlers from Antioquia.
The Nevado del Ruiz, about 5,320 m, rises some 30 km south-east of the city.
The area is part of the Coffee Cultural Landscape of Colombia, a UNESCO site since 2011.

q.q: Which snowy volcano looms over Manizales?

Q518431.t: An anchovy boomtown on a desert bay
Q518431.s: Chimbote curves around a sheltered bay on Peru's bone-dry coast, with rocky islands at its mouth. In the 1960s it boomed as few towns ever have: the cold Humboldt Current teemed with anchovies, and Chimbote became one of the biggest fishing ports in the world. Just to the north, the Santa River brings a green valley down from the Andes.
Q518431.w: A city around a bay with islands at its mouth, on bare desert coast; a green river valley just to the north.
f: Most of the anchovy catch landed here is turned into fishmeal for animal feed.
The Santa River, fed by the glaciers of the Cordillera Blanca, flows all year.
The bay is also known as Ferrol Bay.

q.q: Which fish made Chimbote a boomtown?

Q328846.t: Founded by those who chose to stay Mexican
Q328846.s: When the war of 1846–48 turned the Rio Grande into the border, Laredo ended up in the United States. Some of its families refused to change country: they crossed to the south bank and founded Nuevo Laredo in 1848. Today the two Laredos, joined by several bridges, form the busiest trade crossing on the whole border.
Q328846.w: A city on the south bank of a looping river, facing Laredo; flat, dry brush country all around.
f: Nuevo Laredo was founded in 1848 by families who wanted to remain Mexican.
The city belongs to the state of Tamaulipas.
More US–Mexico trade passes through the two Laredos than any other crossing.

q.q: Why was Nuevo Laredo founded in 1848?

Q187805.t: Waterfalls downtown, flood-scoured land to the south-west
Q187805.s: Spokane grew around a set of waterfalls right in the city centre, where the Spokane River drops through basalt ledges. Look south-west and you'll see a strange landscape of bare channels and scattered lakes: the Channeled Scablands, gouged by colossal floods at the end of the last ice age. Father's Day was first celebrated here, in 1910.
Q187805.w: A city on a river among pine-covered hills; to the south-west, dark scoured channels and small lakes; wheat fields to the south.
f: Father's Day was first celebrated in Spokane in June 1910.
When Spokane hosted the 1974 World's Fair, it was the smallest city ever to have done so.
The Ice Age floods that carved the Scablands burst out of glacial Lake Missoula, in today's Montana.

q.q: Which holiday was first celebrated in Spokane in 1910?

Q23551.t: A university town under Venezuela's highest peaks
Q23551.s: Mérida sits on a long, flat terrace in the deep valley of the Chama River, at about 1,600 m, walled in by two high ranges of the Venezuelan Andes. To the south-east tower the country's highest mountains, led by Pico Bolívar. A cable car climbs from the edge of town almost to the summits. Students of the old University of the Andes fill the streets.
Q23551.w: A city on a long, flat terrace in a deep valley between two high ranges; bare rocky peaks to the south-east.
f: Pico Bolívar, about 4,980 m, is the highest mountain in Venezuela.
The Mukumbarí cable car rises from the city to Pico Espejo at about 4,765 m.
The Coromoto ice-cream parlour once held a world record for the most flavours on sale.

q.q: Which mountain, towering over Mérida, is Venezuela's highest?

Q651906.t: Capital of the backlands of northern Minas
Q651906.s: North of the mining towns of Minas Gerais, the land grows drier and wider: this is the sertão, a country of cerrado scrub, cattle and dry-season dust. Montes Claros is its biggest city and its market town, a crossroads of highways and trade. These backlands are the setting of one of Brazil's greatest novels, Guimarães Rosa's Grande Sertão: Veredas.
Q651906.w: A city on a broad plain between low ridges, amid brownish cerrado in the dry season that turns green in the rains.
f: Montes Claros means 'clear hills'.
It is the largest city in the north of Minas Gerais.
Pequi, a pungent cerrado fruit, is cooked with rice and chicken throughout the region.

q.q: Which famous Brazilian novel is set in the northern Minas backlands?

Q49225.t: The Biggest Little City, at the Sierra's dry foot
Q49225.s: On the dry, eastern side of the Sierra Nevada, Reno fills a high basin at about 1,370 m. Through downtown flows the Truckee River, which leaves Lake Tahoe just over the mountains and ends in Pyramid Lake in the desert, never reaching the sea. An arch over the main street proudly calls Reno 'The Biggest Little City in the World'.
Q49225.w: A city in a high desert basin at the eastern foot of forested mountains; a river winding east, Lake Tahoe hidden beyond the ridge.
f: Pyramid Lake, where the Truckee ends, has no outlet to the sea.
In the 1930s Reno became famous for quick divorces, after Nevada cut residency to six weeks.
Lake Tahoe lies only about 35 km south-west, on the other side of the Carson Range.

q.q: Which lake does the Truckee River flow out of?

Q192235.t: Where three countries meet by a mighty dam
Q192235.s: Two big rivers meet just south of here, and three countries touch: Paraguay, Brazil and Argentina. Ciudad del Este, Paraguay's second city, faces Brazil across the Paraná, joined by the Friendship Bridge, and its streets are crowded with shoppers from across the border. Just upstream stands the Itaipú Dam, and a short way south thunder the Iguazu Falls.
Q192235.w: A city on the west bank of a wide river facing Brazil; a huge reservoir behind a dam just to the north.
f: The Itaipú Dam, shared by Paraguay and Brazil, is one of the largest hydroelectric plants in the world.
The Friendship Bridge across the Paraná links the city with Foz do Iguaçu in Brazil.
Ciudad del Este was founded only in 1957.

q.q: Which huge dam lies just north of Ciudad del Este?

Q109188.t: Salt beef, sweet pastries and two vast lagoons
Q109188.s: Pelotas lies on a flat plain beside the channel that links Brazil's two great coastal lagoons, the Lagoa dos Patos and the Lagoa Mirim. In the 19th century its salt-beef works made it one of the richest towns in the country, and the wealth built grand mansions. Its Portuguese-style egg and sugar sweets are still famous.
Q109188.w: A flat city on a channel between two huge lagoons; the enormous Lagoa dos Patos stretching to the north-east.
f: The name comes from pelotas, small boats of stretched hide once used to cross the rivers.
The sweets of Pelotas were declared part of Brazil's cultural heritage in 2018.
The Lagoa dos Patos is the largest coastal lagoon in Brazil.

q.q: What were the 'pelotas' that gave the city its name?

Q217071.t: Where the road from Lima meets the rivers of the Amazon
Q217071.s: The Ucayali twists across the green plain in huge loops, leaving behind crescent-shaped lakes wherever it changes course. Pucallpa sits on its bank, at the point where the long road over the Andes from Lima finally reaches a river that ships can follow to the Amazon. Right next to the city lies Yarinacocha, an old river bend turned into a lake.
Q217071.w: A wide brown river looping wildly across green forest, with crescent lakes everywhere; the city on its bank beside one of them.
f: Yarinacocha, the oxbow lake on the city's northern edge, was once a bend of the Ucayali.
Riverboats sail from Pucallpa down the Ucayali to Iquitos, a trip of several days.
The Shipibo-Konibo people are known for kené, intricate geometric patterns on cloth and pottery.

q.q: On which river does Pucallpa stand?

Q22062839.t: A cool plateau city in the Bahian backlands
Q22062839.s: Vitória da Conquista stands on a plateau at about 900 m in south-western Bahia, and that height gives it cool nights that surprise visitors to north-eastern Brazil. Coffee grows on the surrounding hills. It is the third-largest city in Bahia and a crossroads on the highway between the north-east and the south. Film-maker Glauber Rocha was born here.
Q22062839.w: A city on a high plateau of farms and coffee plantations; the land drops away to lower, drier country around it.
f: Glauber Rocha, a leader of Brazil's Cinema Novo, was born here in 1939.
At about 900 m, it is one of the coolest cities in north-eastern Brazil.
It is Bahia's third-largest city, after Salvador and Feira de Santana.

q.q: Which film-maker was born in Vitória da Conquista?

Q172512.t: A railway built for rubber, on the Amazon's big tributary
Q172512.s: Porto Velho grew up where boats on the Madeira River met a stretch of rapids they could not pass. To get Bolivian rubber around them, a railway was cut through the jungle, finished in 1912. The capital of Rondônia now sits beside a big hydroelectric dam, and around it the forest is cut into long clearings like the bones of a fish.
Q172512.w: A city on the east bank of a wide brown river, a dam just upstream; forest cut into fishbone-shaped clearings around it.
f: The Madeira–Mamoré Railway, finished in 1912, ran about 366 km around the rapids.
The Madeira is the Amazon's largest tributary.
The Santo Antônio hydroelectric dam stands at the edge of the city.

q.q: Which river flows past Porto Velho?

Q39178.t: Carnival capital between mountains and a calm gulf
Q39178.s: Port of Spain lies on the calm Gulf of Paria, with the forested Northern Range rising right behind it. Just north of downtown, look for a big green oval: the Queen's Park Savannah, heart of one of the world's great carnivals. Trinidad gave the world the steelpan, an instrument hammered out of oil drums. Venezuela is only a short hop across the water.
Q39178.w: A city on a calm gulf at the foot of forested mountains; a large green oval north of downtown, mangrove swamp to the south.
f: The steelpan, made from oil drums, was invented in Trinidad in the 20th century.
At the Dragon's Mouths, Trinidad is only about 11 km from the coast of Venezuela.
The Caroni Swamp, just south of the city, is famous for flocks of scarlet ibis at dusk.

q.q: Which musical instrument was invented in Trinidad?

Q242906.t: Stone goblets on the grassy plains of Paraná
Q242906.s: Ponta Grossa lies on the Campos Gerais, rolling natural grasslands on a high plateau of Paraná. Its name, 'big point', recalls a wooded hill that stood out on the open plain. The city grew as a stop on the old cattle trail to São Paulo. Nearby, in Vila Velha State Park, wind and rain have sculpted sandstone into towers, one shaped like a giant goblet.
Q242906.w: A city on rolling open grassland with dark patches of pine plantations; a low escarpment to the east.
f: Vila Velha State Park's sandstone pillars include one known as 'the Cup'.
The park also has deep water-filled sinkholes called furnas.
Drovers taking mules from the south to Sorocaba once rested their herds here.

q.q: What is Vila Velha State Park near Ponta Grossa known for?

Q54886.t: Where Panama hats are actually made
Q54886.s: Cuenca sits in a green Andean basin at about 2,550 m, crossed by four rivers, and its colonial centre is a UNESCO World Heritage site. Here's a surprise: the famous Panama hat comes from here and the surrounding towns, woven from toquilla straw. It got its name because it was sold to travellers and canal workers in Panama. West of the city, the Cajas moors glitter with lakes.
Q54886.w: A city in a green mountain basin crossed by several rivers; high moorland dotted with small lakes to the west.
f: Cuenca's historic centre has been on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 1999.
The Inca built a major city here called Tomebamba before the Spanish arrived.
Cajas National Park, just west, holds more than 200 lakes and ponds.

q.q: Which famous hat is actually made in and around Cuenca?

Q49242.t: Behind the longest barrier island on Earth
Q49242.s: Look along the Texas coast for a thin ribbon of sand that seems to go on forever: Padre Island, the longest barrier island in the world. Corpus Christi sits on a round bay sheltered behind its northern end. Between the island and the mainland lies the shallow, salty Laguna Madre. On the quiet beaches, rare sea turtles come ashore to lay eggs.
Q49242.w: A round bay behind a thin sandy island that runs far to the south; a narrow lagoon between the island and the mainland.
f: Padre Island stretches about 180 km along the Texas coast.
Padre Island National Seashore is the main US nesting beach of the Kemp's ridley sea turtle.
Tradition says the bay was named on the feast of Corpus Christi in 1519.

q.q: Which long barrier island lies off Corpus Christi?

Q842143.t: Grapes and mangoes in the heart of the dry backlands
Q842143.s: In the grey-brown scrub of Brazil's semi-arid north-east, a blaze of green appears along the São Francisco River: irrigated vineyards and mango orchards. Petrolina, on the Pernambuco bank, faces its twin Juazeiro across the river. With sun almost every day and water from the river, vines here can give more than two harvests a year.
Q842143.w: Bright green irrigated fields along a big river in brownish scrubland; twin cities joined by a bridge; a vast reservoir upstream.
f: Mangoes and grapes from this valley are exported to Europe and North America.
Upstream, the Sobradinho reservoir is one of the largest artificial lakes in the world by area.
The valley also makes wine, unusual so close to the equator.

q.q: Which city faces Petrolina across the São Francisco River?

Q171612.t: A rubber town that joined Brazil in 1903
Q171612.s: Rio Branco grew on the meandering Acre River, deep in the western Amazon, from a rubber-tapping settlement of the 1880s. Back then this land was claimed by Bolivia; it became Brazilian by treaty in 1903, and the city was named after the diplomat who negotiated it, the Baron of Rio Branco. Today it is the capital of Acre.
Q171612.w: A city on a winding river in the rainforest, surrounded by cattle pastures cut out of the forest.
f: The Treaty of Petrópolis, signed in 1903, made Acre part of Brazil.
The city began in 1882 as a rubber estate on the Acre River.
The Santo Daime religion was founded near Rio Branco in the 1930s.

q.q: Which country did Acre belong to before 1903?

Q80517.t: Named after the man who cleared a giant logjam
Q80517.s: For centuries a vast tangle of fallen trees, the Great Raft, choked the Red River for well over 200 km. In the 1830s Captain Henry Shreve cleared it with his snag boats, opening the river to steamboats, and the town that sprang up was named after him. Shreveport faces Bossier City across the rust-coloured river, amid pine forests and lakes.
Q80517.w: A city on a winding, reddish-brown river with oxbow lakes, surrounded by pine forest; a large lake just west of downtown.
f: Henry Shreve's snag boats pulled apart the Great Raft logjam in the 1830s.
Elvis Presley made some of his first broadcasts on Shreveport's Louisiana Hayride in 1954.
The Red River takes its colour from the reddish soils it carries.

q.q: What did Henry Shreve clear from the Red River?

Q44239.t: Two rivers join to make one, in dinosaur country
Q44239.s: In the brown Patagonian steppe, two rivers from the Andes meet — the Limay and the Neuquén — and together become the Río Negro. Neuquén sits right at the fork, at the head of a green strip of apple and pear orchards. The province is famous for giants: some of the largest dinosaurs ever found were dug up here.
